The Sun is too cold to shine... and yet, it does.
Its core is fifteen million degrees, which sounds hot.
But to fuse, two protons have to touch, and protons push each other away with enormous force.
By ordinary physics, forcing them together should take billions of degrees. The Sun is hundreds of times too cold.
So how does it burn? The protons cheat.
It's called quantum tunnelling. A particle is also a wave, and a little of that wave leaks straight through the wall.
Even then, it almost never works, because in that same instant, one proton has to turn into a neutron.
So an average proton waits nine billion years for its turn. Litre for litre, your body makes more heat than the Sun's core.
But the Sun is enormous. So every sunbeam you've ever felt began with a particle walking through a wall.
